prize_parts.citation: For the development of targeted protein degradation, in which small molecules recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases to destroy chosen proteins.

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation is a genuinely new chemical concept: a designed molecule brings a target and an E3 ligase together so the target is ubiquitylated and destroyed catalytically, an event-driven mode of action that reaches proteins long considered undruggable. It is the one candidate that six of eight members placed in their top three, and the support comes from members with quite different backgrounds, which is more informative than a single enthusiastic champion. The PROTAC concept (Crews and Deshaies, 2001) and the later structure-guided, VHL-based design work (Ciulli, with Crews) give a coherent three-person story for the degrader chemistry, and many independent groups and clinical-stage compounds confirm it. I continue to regard the Car-Parrinello method (B053) as the cleanest piece of science on the list and would rank it first on pure originality and four decades of impact, but it has one first-place vote and almost no other support, and I should not mistake my own field affinity for committee-wide merit.
statement.case_against: The largest weakness is attribution. A three-name trio built around PROTACs leaves out Handa, Ito and the cereblon/thalidomide molecular-glue strand, which is arguably the part with the most patient benefit so far, as well as Sakamoto, Kim and Gray. Maturity is also a concern: no degrader drug has yet been approved, so the clinical payoff is promised rather than shown. If the committee cannot settle on a defensible split, this is a prize that could look rushed or incomplete in a few years, and a well-established, fully mature achievement such as B053 or B059 would carry less risk.

responses.point: Linke ranks degradation first as a new small-molecule pharmacology, with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli as the core, and accepts that the molecular-glue strand would be left out; he also ranks Solexa sequencing second as a fully mature, overdue analytical-chemistry achievement.
responses.response: I agree on the conceptual originality and on the trio, but I would not wave away the glue omission as lightly as the opening suggests. If the citation is worded around induced-proximity degraders in general, then leaving out the cereblon discoverers invites the criticism that the prize rewards the engineered version of a mechanism others uncovered. I would keep the citation narrow, on bifunctional degrader design, to match the three names. On B014 I disagree mildly that overdue means ready: sequencing credit is split across Solexa, 454 and others, and a two-person Balasubramanian-Klenerman prize would exclude Rothberg, which the committee would have to defend.

responses.point: Brzezinski ranks perovskite solar cells first for its rapid, independently certified efficiency gains, and prefers a degradation trio of Crews, Deshaies and Handa to cover both the PROTAC and cereblon strands.
responses.response: I take the Crews-Deshaies-Handa trio seriously because it spans PROTACs and cereblon, but it drops Ciulli, whose structure-guided work made degraders drug-like and who is the most convincing link between mechanism and design. I would pick Ciulli over Handa for a PROTAC-centred citation and accept that this leaves the glue story for another year. On perovskites (B005), I think the science is real but six credited names, contested priority among Miyasaka, Park, Snaith, Grätzel and Seok, and open questions about stability and toxicity make it a weaker candidate for now than the degradation field.

responses.point: Somfai ranks Pd-catalyzed C-N coupling first, arguing that Buchwald and Hartwig developed it in parallel, that Kosugi's tin-amide work was only a proof of concept, and that recognition is overdue.
responses.response: I agree that Buchwald and Hartwig are the clean pair and that the work is mature and widely used, which is why I keep B059 as an alternative. My reservation is the 2010 cross-coupling prize: the committee would have to explain why C-N coupling is a distinct achievement and not a continuation of Heck, Negishi and Suzuki, and I would want that argument made explicitly before ranking it above a new modality. I do not think the Kosugi and Migita precedent is disqualifying, but it needs to be addressed in the citation or the discussion.

responses.point: Chabes ranks massively parallel sequencing first, stressing the nucleotide chemistry of reversible terminators, and ranks degradation second while saying the PROTAC and glue halves are at different stages of maturity.
responses.response: I share his view that the two halves of this field are at different stages, and that is the main reason I regard B020 as promising but not risk-free. Where I differ is on B014: the chemistry is real, but the effect on sequencing came from engineering and commercial scale-up as much as from a single chemical idea, and the credit among Solexa, 454 and Mayer/Ju is unsettled. I would want the committee to decide whether it is rewarding the reversible-terminator chemistry specifically before treating this as overdue.

uncertainties: Whether a PROTAC-centred trio can be defended without Handa and Ito, or whether the committee should split the prize between PROTACs and cereblon-based molecular glues.
Whether the absence of an approved degrader drug makes the timing premature relative to mature candidates such as B053 or B059.
How the committee would treat the 2010 cross-coupling prize if B059 moved up.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B020. My postdoc connection with Arieh Warshel and my work in biomolecular simulation make me close to the computational field of B053 and the folding-theory field of B050, but none of the credited individuals is a collaborator, so I do not see a recusal issue.
